meta.blurb: A rich old merchant is shot dead in his locked library, and the evidence points to the beautiful niece a young lawyer has come to love. With a clever detective, he follows a secret marriage, a missing maid and a forged letter to the truth.
meta.bible: Everett Raymond: the young lawyer who tells the story; honest, loyal, falls in love with Eleanore. Horatio Leavenworth: the rich old New York merchant, shot dead in his library; he hated the English. Mary Leavenworth: his niece and the heiress; proud, beautiful and secretly married. Eleanore Leavenworth: his other niece; proud, loyal, protects her cousin. Trueman Harwell: Mr Leavenworth's secretary, stiff and silent, in love with Mary; the murderer. Ebenezer Gryce: the police detective, sly, polite, with rheumatism. Henry Ritchie Clavering: the Englishman who is Mary's secret husband. Hannah Chester: the Irish maid who vanishes the night of the murder and dies. Mr Veeley: Mr Leavenworth's old friend and Raymond's senior partner. Mrs Amy Belden: a kind widow in a country village who hides Hannah. Q: Gryce's young helper. Thomas: the butler. Katherine Malone: the cook. Timothy Cook: the minister's hired man who saw the wedding. Fifth Avenue: the street of the Leavenworth house. New York. England. Hoffman House. Voice and tone: a lawyer's first-person story told in plain and clever steps, a fair puzzle with a surprise at the end; the death is stated plainly and without gore; set in 1870s New York.

beats.scene: A pale young man hurries into a lawyer's office in New York
beats.summary: Harwell, the secretary, tells young lawyer Everett Raymond that Mr Leavenworth has been shot dead.

beats.scene: Raymond pushes through a crowd to the steps of a great Fifth Avenue house
beats.summary: Raymond and Harwell reach the house on Fifth Avenue, where the detective Ebenezer Gryce lets them in.

beats.scene: Gryce draws back the bed curtains to show a calm, still face
beats.summary: Gryce shows Raymond the dead man and says that the wound could not have been made by Mr Leavenworth himself.

beats.scene: A quiet library with a long writing table, a lamp and one locked door
beats.summary: Mr Leavenworth was shot at his library table; the library door was locked and its key was missing; his own pistol was used.

beats.scene: A coroner and jurors listen to the secretary in a crowded parlour
beats.summary: At the inquest, Harwell says he drank sherry with Mr Leavenworth and later heard a lady's dress rustle in the hall.

beats.scene: A round-faced cook twists her apron in front of the stern coroner
beats.summary: The cook lets slip the name of Hannah, a maid who has vanished since the night before.

beats.scene: Doctors and officials examine a small pistol and a bullet on a table
beats.summary: Experts show that Mr Leavenworth's own pistol was fired from behind by someone inside the house.

beats.scene: Two lovely young women in black wait together in a grand drawing room
beats.summary: Mary and Eleanore, the orphaned nieces, are described; Eleanore is questioned and her guarded answers seem to hide something.

beats.scene: Gryce holds up a stained white handkerchief marked with the letters E L
beats.summary: Gryce produces Eleanore's handkerchief, stained with pistol grease and found in the library; she grows pale.

beats.scene: Mary, in black, speaks softly to Raymond in a corner of the parlour
beats.summary: Mary begs Raymond to warn Eleanore that her guarded manner is arousing suspicion, and he cannot tell if her fear is real.

beats.scene: Gryce holds up the library key before Eleanore in a small side room
beats.summary: A witness saw Eleanore drop the library key into the ashes; she admits it but will say nothing more.

beats.scene: Eleanore sits pale in a dim drawing room beside a newspaper on the floor
beats.summary: The newspapers suspect Eleanore; she tells Raymond she is innocent and he resolves to believe her.

beats.scene: Mary points angrily at the door while Eleanore stands facing her
beats.summary: The cousins quarrel, and Mary declares that one of them must leave the house.

beats.scene: Raymond reads a newspaper notice describing a missing maid
beats.summary: A reward is offered for news of Hannah Chester, and Raymond sees that she is the one witness who matters.

beats.scene: A lawyer reads aloud a long will to the family around a table
beats.summary: The will leaves most of the fortune to Mary and a smaller sum to Eleanore.

beats.scene: Gryce, bent over a desk of small drawers, speaks quietly to Raymond
beats.summary: Gryce asks Raymond to find out about Mr Clavering and the quarrel between the cousins; Raymond agrees to help Harwell with the dead man's book.

beats.scene: Mary stands at the foot of the stairs in lamplight, asking a question
beats.summary: Mary asks Raymond whether a person who has done a great wrong can grow to be good.

beats.scene: A stranger whispers fiercely to Mary in the hall while Harwell points at him
beats.summary: A stranger speaks fiercely to Mary, and when Harwell hears his name, Henry Clavering, he cries out that the man is the murderer.

beats.scene: A tall, well-dressed Englishman reads from a notebook in a lawyer's office
beats.summary: Clavering visits Raymond and asks, on behalf of a friend, whether a secret marriage made without a licence is legal.

beats.scene: Harwell stands stiffly before Raymond, taking back his angry words
beats.summary: Harwell apologises for his accusation but says he had a dream in which a man like Clavering lifted a hand against Mr Leavenworth.

beats.scene: A man sits at a window opposite the Leavenworth house, watching its door
beats.summary: Clavering is said to have sailed for Europe, but Gryce knows that he is watching Mary's house from across the street.

beats.scene: An old lawyer sits by a fire, telling a story to a young man
beats.summary: Mr Veeley explains that Mr Leavenworth's wife suffered in a cruel first marriage, which is why he hated every Englishman.

beats.scene: Raymond and Gryce question a hired man outside a small country parsonage
beats.summary: The trail of the secret marriage leads to a country parsonage, where the hired man Timothy Cook was a witness.

beats.scene: The hired man smiles at the memory of a lovely bride in the parsonage
beats.summary: Cook cannot recall the bride's name but describes her so well that Raymond fears it is Mary.

beats.scene: Gryce sits smiling with folded hands while Raymond stares at him in shock
beats.summary: Gryce explains that the angry words they overheard at the inquest were spoken by Eleanore, who suspected Mary.

beats.scene: Raymond paces the floor in anger while Gryce calmly watches him
beats.summary: Raymond refuses to believe Mary is guilty; Gryce says Eleanore's hiding of the key and letter shows what she feared, and that Hannah must be found.

beats.scene: Raymond rides along a country road toward a quiet village
beats.summary: A clue leads Raymond to a village and to Mrs Amy Belden, a widow who knew Mary a year before.

beats.scene: Raymond studies a sunny parlour while a kind widow talks beside him
beats.summary: Mrs Belden welcomes Raymond and chats about Mary, while he searches her house for signs of another person.

beats.scene: A young man dressed as a tramp slips Raymond a note at dawn
beats.summary: Gryce's young helper Q, disguised as a tramp, sends Raymond a note saying that Hannah is in the little back room.

beats.scene: Raymond stands in a small bedroom beside a still figure in a narrow bed
beats.summary: Raymond finds Hannah dead in her bed in the back room.

beats.scene: Raymond draws a folded paper from under the dead girl's shoulder
beats.summary: Under Hannah's body Raymond finds a printed confession that clears Eleanore and points to a dark man like Clavering.

beats.scene: Gryce holds the confession up to the light beside a window curtain
beats.summary: Gryce arrives, studies the paper and declares that the confession is a forgery.

beats.scene: Gryce smiles kindly at the widow beside a table of paper boxes
beats.summary: Mrs Belden reveals that Hannah had learned to write; Gryce concludes that someone sent her both the false confession and the poison.

beats.scene: Gryce lays sheets of paper side by side beside a writing desk
beats.summary: Gryce compares the ruled lines of the confession with paper from the library table in Mary's house and finds a perfect match.

beats.scene: A dim garret room with a pine table, two chairs and many closed doors
beats.summary: Gryce leads Raymond to a bare garret room with ventilators over the doors and tells him to stay silent.

beats.scene: Gryce leans toward Raymond, speaking loudly, with closed doors all around
beats.summary: Gryce, speaking as if to a friend named Smith, announces loudly that the murderer is a woman, and that it is Mary.

beats.scene: Harwell bursts into the room, wild-eyed, and rushes at Clavering
beats.summary: Harwell cries out to stop the report, and when Clavering appears he flies at him in a fury and collapses.

beats.scene: A man at a prison table writes in the lamplight with his head bowed
beats.summary: In prison, Harwell writes a full confession, saying that he is an intense man who has always loved Mary and been overlooked by everyone.

beats.scene: Harwell opens a letter at a desk while a stern old man sits nearby
beats.summary: Harwell opens Clavering's letter to Mr Leavenworth and decides to let him read it, hoping the quarrel will give him a hold on Mary.

beats.scene: A secretary listens at a closet while Mary pleads in the room below
beats.summary: On the night of the murder Harwell hears Mary beg her uncle to forgive her, and hears Mr Leavenworth refuse and say he will change his will.

beats.scene: A man stands behind a seated old man writing at a lamp-lit table
beats.summary: Harwell fetches the pistol, shoots Mr Leavenworth, and takes the unfinished letter and Clavering's letter.

beats.scene: Harwell meets the frightened maid Hannah at the top of the stairs
beats.summary: Harwell cleans the pistol with Eleanore's handkerchief, locks the door, and is seen by Hannah, whom he sends away to Mrs Belden with a promise.

beats.scene: A candle-lit key and charred scraps hidden near a gas lamp and a vase
beats.summary: Harwell hides the key and burns the letters, and at the inquest he lies, so that suspicion falls on Eleanore.

beats.scene: Harwell watches a stranger in the hall who calls Mary his wife
beats.summary: Harwell hears Clavering call Mary his wife, accuses him of the murder in a fury, and then decides to put the blame on him.

beats.scene: A man seals a letter at night while a candle burns low
beats.summary: Harwell sends Hannah a letter with a charm and poison and a forged confession, knowing she will swallow it.

beats.scene: Raymond leans toward Eleanore, who sits pale in a quiet drawing room
beats.summary: Raymond tells Eleanore that the murderer was Harwell, not Mary, and she asks to be taken to her cousin at once.

beats.scene: Two cousins embrace in the doorway of a drawing room
beats.summary: Eleanore and Mary meet in the drawing room, forgive one another and end the old shadow between them.

beats.scene: Mary hands a folded paper to Eleanore while Raymond looks on
beats.summary: Mary offers her whole fortune to Eleanore; Eleanore refuses money stained by guilt, and they decide that it will go to charity.

beats.scene: Clavering offers his hand to Raymond in a lamp-lit drawing room
beats.summary: Clavering apologises to Raymond for the insulting document he forced on him, and the two men become friends.

beats.scene: Raymond and Eleanore walk out together into the night
beats.summary: Raymond and Eleanore go to tell Mr Veeley the truth, and Raymond later marries her.

B1B2: Everett Raymond, a young lawyer in New York, is alone in the office when a worried man hurries in. He is Trueman Harwell, secretary to the rich Mr Leavenworth, and he says that his employer was shot in the night.

A large crowd has gathered outside the great house on Fifth Avenue, and Raymond has to push his way through to the steps. At the door he is met by Ebenezer Gryce, a police detective whom he already knows.

Gryce leads Raymond upstairs to the bedroom, where Mr Leavenworth lies as if he were asleep. The wound at the back of the head, the detective says quietly, could never have been made by the man himself.
Mr Leavenworth was shot as he sat at the table in his library late at night. The door of the room was found locked in the morning, and its key could not be found anywhere.
Harwell tells the inquest that he and his employer drank a glass of sherry together late that evening. Soon after he went upstairs, he says, he heard a lady's dress rustle along the hall.

The cook, Katherine Malone, lets the name of Hannah slip out and then tries to take it back. At last she admits that the lady's maid has vanished since the night before, though her clothes are still in the house.

Doctors and gun experts agree that Mr Leavenworth was shot from behind with his own pistol. Only one bullet had been fired, and since the house was locked all night, it must have been fired by someone inside.

The two nieces, Mary and Eleanore, had lived with their uncle for many years, and both are young and beautiful. When Eleanore is questioned, her careful and strange answers make the people in the room wonder what she is hiding.

Gryce holds up a handkerchief that was found in the library, marked with Eleanore's initials and stained with pistol grease. She has said that she did not enter that room for a whole day, and now she turns white.
Mary, weeping, whispers to Raymond that Eleanore's manner has made people suspect her. She says the two cousins are not friends, and Raymond cannot decide whether her tears are real.
Gryce shows Eleanore the key to the library door, which a man saw her drop into the ashes of a fire. She does not deny it, but she refuses to explain why she hid it.

The newspapers now say that a member of the family is suspected, and Raymond finds Eleanore alone and shaken in the dim drawing room. She tells him that she is innocent, and he promises himself that he will believe her.
When the cousins meet, the anger between them is so strong that Raymond leaves the room. Soon afterwards Mary comes out in tears and says that the same roof cannot shelter them both.
A newspaper notice offers a reward for news of Hannah Chester, the maid who vanished on the night of the murder. Raymond decides that she is the one person whose story could solve the whole case.
The will is printed in the morning newspaper, and it surprises Raymond. Most of the great fortune goes to Mary, while Eleanore receives only a smaller sum that was added years before.

Gryce asks Raymond to find out how a Mr Clavering is connected with the two ladies, and why the cousins dislike each other. Raymond refuses to spy, but he agrees to help Harwell finish his dead employer's book.
One evening Mary stops Raymond at the foot of the stairs with a strange question. She asks whether a person who has done something very wrong can still grow to be good.

One evening Raymond and Harwell see a stranger speaking to Mary in a low, fierce voice. When Harwell hears the man's name, Henry Clavering, he suddenly cries out that he is the murderer of Mr Leavenworth.

The next day Clavering visits Raymond's office and asks for advice on behalf of a friend. This friend, he says, married an American girl in secret, and he wants to know whether the marriage was legal.
Harwell comes to apologise for his angry words, but he cannot explain them. He says that he once dreamed of a man like Clavering raising a hand against his employer, and Raymond cannot forget it.
Everyone is told that Clavering has sailed for Europe, but Gryce knows better. The Englishman has only changed rooms, and from a window across the street he watches Mary's door.
Mr Veeley, the old family friend, tells Raymond why Mr Leavenworth could not bear the word Englishman. His beloved wife had suffered terribly in a cruel first marriage, and she died young.
Raymond and Gryce trace the secret marriage to a parsonage in a small country town. The Methodist minister has died, but his hired man, Timothy Cook, remembers the wedding well.
Cook cannot remember the bride's name, but he says her face was so sweet that he could never forget it. As he describes her, Raymond fears that the lady is Mary Leavenworth.

Gryce reminds Raymond of an angry sentence they overheard on the morning of the inquest, which Raymond believed was Mary's. With a smile, he explains that it was Eleanore who spoke, because she suspected her cousin.
Raymond refuses to believe that a woman like Mary could have done such a thing. Gryce replies that this explains why Eleanore hid the key and the letter, and he says that Hannah must be found.
At last a clue leads Raymond to a quiet country village and to a kind widow named Amy Belden. A year earlier Mary used to visit her, and Hannah carried messages between Mary and her secret lover.
Mrs Belden welcomes Raymond warmly and talks about Mary's visits, but she says nothing of Hannah. Raymond studies the sunny room and the little yard, and he hears soft footsteps overhead.
Q, Gryce's young helper, comes to the house dressed as a tramp, and Mrs Belden lets him sleep in the kitchen. Before dawn he slips Raymond a note that says Hannah is in the small back room upstairs.
When the widow has gone out, Raymond climbs the stairs and enters the small back room. Hannah lies in the bed, peaceful and cold, and he sees that she has been dead for some hours.

Raymond sees the corner of an envelope under the dead girl's shoulder and draws it out. It holds a confession in rough printed letters, clearing Eleanore and describing a dark man who sounds like Clavering.
Gryce arrives, limping and ill, and asks exactly how the letter lay under the body. After studying it closely, he says that the confession is a fraud and that Hannah never wrote it.

Gryce questions Mrs Belden with great kindness, and she tells him that Hannah learned to write in her house. The rough printing could not be Hannah's, and a thick letter had come for her the day before.
Gryce searches Eleanore's desk first and finds nothing at all. Then he takes a pile of paper from the library table in Mary's house, and its lines fit the confession exactly.
Gryce leads Raymond to a bare room at the top of his house, with a dirty skylight and closed doors. He tells Raymond to stay silent, and not to be surprised by anything that he says.
Gryce calls Raymond 'Smith' and announces in a loud voice that he has found the murderer and that it is a woman. He says that it is Mary, and that a report is already on its way to the police.
Harwell bursts out of a hiding place and begs them to stop the report and save Mary. When Henry Clavering steps into the room, Harwell flies at him in a fury, and then he falls to the floor.
In prison, Harwell writes down the whole truth about himself. He says that nobody ever understood him, and that from the first evening he loved Mary, who never looked at him.
Harwell learns of Mary's secret from a letter from Clavering. He hands it to Mr Leavenworth on purpose, hoping that the quarrel will give him some power over Mary.
That night Harwell hears Mary go down to the library, and he listens through a ventilator. She begs her uncle to forgive her, but he refuses and says he is changing his will.
After Mary has gone up, Harwell goes down to the library and fetches the pistol from the bedroom. He shoots Mr Leavenworth, then takes the letter that the old man was writing and Clavering's letter.
Harwell cleans the pistol with Eleanore's handkerchief and puts it back. At the door he is seen by Hannah, so he promises to marry her and sends her away to Mrs Belden.
Harwell hides the key and the letters in the house and tries to destroy them. At the inquest he lies to protect himself, and the suspicion falls on Eleanore.

When Harwell hears Clavering call Mary his wife, he is mad with jealousy and accuses him of the murder. Afterwards he decides that the blame should fall on Clavering, and that Hannah must not be allowed to speak.
Harwell writes to Hannah in printed letters, telling her that she should take a charm to bring good dreams. He encloses a poison powder and a false confession, and soon afterwards she dies.
Raymond hurries to Eleanore with good news, and she is afraid to believe it. When she learns that Harwell, not Mary, was the murderer, she begs to be taken to her cousin at once.
Raymond takes Eleanore to Mary's house, where the two cousins meet in the doorway. Eleanore falls at her cousin's feet, and the long shadow between them melts like a cloud.
Mary, softened and humble, offers to give her fortune to Eleanore. Eleanore will not take money so stained by crime, so they agree to use it to build a charity for the poor of the city.
Henry Clavering takes Raymond aside and apologises for a document that he had once forced upon him. Raymond tells him that the past should be forgotten, and the two men become friends.
Mary wants to tell Mr Veeley the truth, but Eleanore says that Mary has suffered enough. She and Raymond go out into the night together, and later they are married.
C1C2: On a spring morning, while both of his partners were away, the young lawyer Everett Raymond looked up to find a pale and hurried stranger standing in the doorway of his office. The man introduced himself coolly as Trueman Harwell, private secretary to Mr Leavenworth, and announced in a flat, businesslike voice that his employer had been shot through the head at his own library table. Since the family's old friend Mr Veeley was out of town, the two young ladies of the house had no one to advise them, and Raymond felt bound to go in his place.

The mansion on Fifth Avenue stood surrounded by a restless crowd of idlers, errand boys and reporters, all hoping for some glimpse of the tragedy within. Raymond forced a path to the stone steps behind Harwell and rang the bell, and the door was opened at once by Ebenezer Gryce, a police detective whose face he knew well. Gryce drew them quickly inside with a grim little smile, shut out the disappointed faces, and told them that the coroner's inquest was about to begin.

In the great bedroom upstairs, Gryce drew back the heavy curtains of the bed and revealed a face so calm that Raymond started, for death had not twisted a single feature. The wound at the back of the skull, the detective remarked, was of a kind that could never have been made by the dead man's own hand, and no surgeon would think otherwise. It was, he said with perfect composure, a case of deliberate murder.

The library, where the old merchant had spent his last evening, lay at the back of the house, with a long writing table, a shaded lamp and a single door that opened on the hall. When the household gathered there the next morning, they found that door locked and the key gone, so that the room itself seemed to guard its secret. The pistol that had done the deed was no stranger to the house, for it belonged to Mr Leavenworth himself and was kept in his own bedroom.

In the large parlour below, the coroner and a jury of solemn citizens listened while Harwell, steady and precise as ever, described the last hour he had spent with his employer. He had shared a glass of sherry with Mr Leavenworth, he said, wished him good night and gone upstairs, and only a few minutes later had heard the soft rustle of a lady's dress passing along the passage. Everyone in the room took it for granted that the sound had been made by one of the two nieces.

Katherine Malone, the plump and anxious cook, let slip the name of a servant called Hannah, and then tried, too late, to pretend that it had meant nothing. Under the coroner's stern questions she admitted that the girl had gone up to the attic bedroom at ten o'clock, yet that her bed was empty in the morning, and her clothes were still hanging where she had left them. A hush fell over the room, as though a door had suddenly opened in a solid wall.

The surgeons explained to the jury that the bullet had entered the back of the dead man's head at a slight angle, which showed that he had been bending forward over his writing. Experts who examined the pistol found that a single shot had lately been fired from it, and that the bullet taken from the wound fitted the weapon exactly. Since every door of the house had been locked all night, it followed that the person who had pulled the trigger had been under the same roof as the sleeping family.

The old merchant's two orphaned nieces, Mary and Eleanore, had grown up under his roof, and either of them might have been called the loveliest woman in New York. Mary was expected to inherit the greater part of his fortune, but it was Eleanore whom the coroner questioned longest, because her answers were so guarded and so oddly chosen. Raymond, watching her proud, pale face, felt a pity that he could not yet explain.

Mr Gryce then produced a small white handkerchief that had been found in the library, soiled with the dark grease of a pistol and marked in one corner with the initials E L. Eleanore, who had firmly declared that she had not entered that room for a whole day before the murder, grew pale to the lips and could not at first find a word to say. Raymond saw the sudden change in her face and felt a chill of dread that he tried at once to push away.

Mary Leavenworth, weeping in a corner of the parlour, begged Raymond to warn her cousin that her guarded manner was creating dangerous suspicions. She protested, in a whisper that carried across the room, that she and Eleanore were no friends, yet she would never believe that the girl knew anything of the crime. Raymond studied her tearful face with astonishment, unable to decide whether he was watching real fear or the most polished acting he had ever seen.

Gryce had in his hand the missing key of the library door, and he told Eleanore that a witness had seen her drop it into the ashes of a grate. With a look full of suffering and a certain courage, she answered that he was quite right, but that nothing in the world would make her say another word on the subject. Raymond, who had longed to hear a denial, could only watch her walk out of the room with her head held high.

The next day's newspapers hinted openly that a member of the dead man's own family was suspected, and Raymond found Eleanore sitting alone in the half-lit drawing room, as still and white as a marble statue. She looked up at him with a mixture of terror and appeal, and when she declared that she was innocent of her uncle's death, every doubt in his mind melted away. From that hour he resolved that he would clear her name, whatever it might cost him.

The two cousins met face to face in the drawing room, and the feeling between them was so fierce that Raymond felt he had no right to stand there and hastily withdrew. A few minutes later Mary swept out, flushed and trembling, with the cry that the same roof could never shelter them both and that one of them must find another home by the morrow. Neither Raymond nor anyone else in the house understood the deep distrust that had grown up between two women who ought to have been friends.

The newspapers carried a notice offering a generous reward for any news of Hannah Chester, a young Irish maid who had vanished from the house on the night of the murder. Raymond reflected that no one had paid her much attention, and yet she was surely the one witness whose testimony would decide everything. Why she had run away, and from whom or what, remained a question to which no one could yet give an answer.

The next morning's newspaper printed the main terms of the will, and they came as a surprise to Raymond and to most of the city. The bulk of the great fortune was left to Mary, while Eleanore had received only a modest legacy, added by a codicil some years before, which would keep her in comfort but no more. The public, which loves a motive, began at once to ask whether so unequal a gift could have driven someone to murder.

Gryce invited Raymond to his house and asked him to discover what connection a certain Mr Clavering had with the two ladies, and what had caused the bitterness between the cousins. Raymond, who disliked the idea of acting as a spy in a woman's house, replied that he would listen openly but would never listen at doors. He agreed, however, to help the secretary prepare the dead man's unfinished book for the press, since that would give him a reason to visit the house.

One evening Mary Leavenworth waited for him at the foot of the stairs, and with a look of great embarrassment asked whether a person who had done some serious wrong could grow to be thoroughly good. Raymond answered that it was possible if the person were truly sorry, and that a confession might sometimes make amends for a wrong. She seemed troubled by his answer, and the question lingered in his mind long after he had left the house.

One evening, as Raymond and Harwell came down the stairs together, they saw a strange gentleman standing in the reception room and speaking to Mary Leavenworth in a low and passionate voice. When the secretary learned that the stranger was Henry Clavering, the man whose name had already troubled the household, he lost all his usual calm. To Raymond's amazement, he denounced the newcomer, before everyone present, as the man who had murdered Mr Leavenworth.

On the following morning a tall, well-bred gentleman presented a card that read Henry Ritchie Clavering and said that he wished to consult Raymond about the troubles of a friend. The story, which he read slowly from a notebook, was of an Englishman who had married an American girl in secret, without a licence, before a country clergyman, while she was still under twenty-one. Raymond, who felt a sudden dislike and an even deeper curiosity, wondered how much of this tale belonged to the man sitting in front of him.

Harwell called upon Raymond the next day to apologise for the violence of his words, yet he declined to explain what grounds he could have had for so terrible an accusation. Pressed hard, he admitted that he had dreamed, on the night before the murder, of a man lifting his hand against Mr Leavenworth, and that the face had seemed to him to be Clavering's. Raymond, who was shaken despite himself, felt his own suspicion of the Englishman grow stronger.

Everyone was told that Henry Clavering had sailed for Europe, and Raymond had even spoken to the driver who claimed to have taken him to the ship. Gryce, however, smiled and explained that the Englishman had merely changed his lodgings and now sat, day after day, at a window opposite the Leavenworth house, watching who came and went. It was a strange way for an innocent man to behave, and the detective seemed to find it very interesting indeed.

Mr Veeley, who had known the family for many years, told Raymond how Horatio Leavenworth had once met a young woman in England who had endured a cruel first marriage, and how he had married her out of love. She never recovered from that suffering, he said, and she died two years later, and ever afterwards the very word Englishman was more than her husband could bear. Raymond listened in silence, for he suddenly understood why a secret marriage to an Englishman would have enraged the old man.

Following the thread of Clavering's story, Raymond and the detective traced the secret marriage to a country parsonage, where it had taken place the previous summer before a Methodist clergyman. The minister was now dead, but his hired man, an honest, shock-headed fellow named Timothy Cook, had stood as one of the two witnesses and remembered the day perfectly. Gryce questioned him with his usual gentle cunning, and Raymond waited with a heavy heart to hear the description of the bride.

Cook could not recall the lady's first name, but he declared that she was so handsome that he could never forget her sweet face if he lived for a hundred years. As he described her, a terrible suspicion crept over Raymond, for the portrait that the honest fellow drew was the portrait of a woman he knew. The secret wife of Henry Clavering, it seemed, was no stranger, and Raymond could hardly bear to put her name into words.

Gryce reminded Raymond of an accusation that the two men had overheard between the cousins on the morning of the inquest, and which Raymond had always taken to be Mary's cry against Eleanore. With a smile of quiet triumph, the detective explained that the two voices were so alike that he had let his companion go on believing it, whereas it was Eleanore who had spoken, because she thought that Mary was guilty. Raymond felt an avalanche of doubts fall upon him, and he realised that he had been reading every fact through a terrible mistake.

Raymond paced the floor and protested that no evidence in the world could make him believe that a woman like Mary Leavenworth had committed so cruel and deliberate a crime. Gryce answered dryly that Eleanore must have had her reasons for hiding the key and for trying to burn a letter that exposed her cousin's secret, and that such reasons were not found for nothing. The only person who could settle the matter, he said, was the vanished maid Hannah, and he meant to find her.

At last a slender thread of evidence led Raymond to a quiet country village, and to the cottage of a kindly widow named Amy Belden. A year earlier, he learned, Mary Leavenworth had often visited this lonely woman, who had grown fond of her, and the maid Hannah had carried messages between the lovers in those days. If the missing girl had gone anywhere on the night of the murder, he reasoned, she would surely have gone to the one person who knew the whole secret.

Mrs Belden received the stranger with kindly curiosity, and while she chattered about Mary's visits, Raymond studied every corner of her sunny sitting room for some trace of another occupant. He examined the books, the music and the windows that overlooked the yard, and from time to time he caught the faint sound of steps moving about the floor above. He was now almost certain that the girl he sought was hidden somewhere in the house.

Q, the quick young helper who worked for Gryce, had come to the house the evening before disguised as a ragged tramp, and Mrs Belden, in her kindness, had let him sleep in the kitchen. Before dawn he slipped a note into Raymond's hand which said that Hannah was hidden in the small back room above the dining room, and that he would find some way of drawing the widow out of the house. Raymond, tingling with hope, lay down once more, but he could not sleep a wink.

When the widow had been drawn away, Raymond hurried up the stairs, entered the little back room and found, to his horror, that Hannah lay quiet in her bed, her face so calm that death seemed pleasanter than people think. She had been dead for some hours, and with her had gone every hope of the testimony on which he had built so much. Standing there, he reproached himself bitterly for not having forced his way to her door the night before.

Beneath the dead girl's shoulders Raymond saw the corner of an envelope, and when he drew it out he found a letter printed in rough, childish capitals and meant to be her last confession. It declared that Eleanore was innocent and described a dark gentleman with a black moustache who had made the girl run away, a description that fitted Henry Clavering so closely that Raymond felt a triumphant leap of the heart. He slipped the paper into his coat and waited for Gryce, whom he had summoned by telegram.

Gryce limped in from the train on a single stick, and he examined the letter with an eagerness that quickly turned into delighted surprise. He pointed out that the sheet had been cut down from a larger piece, so that every mark of its maker was gone, and that no dying girl would take such pains to hide where her paper came from. Looking for the first time straight into Raymond's eyes, he announced that the famous confession was a fraud.

With great kindness, Gryce drew from Mrs Belden the fact that Hannah had learned to write in her house, and that a thick letter had reached her on the very day she died. A girl who could write well, he pointed out, would never have printed her last words in clumsy capitals, and a girl who meant to end her life would not have cared where her paper came from. Someone else, he concluded, had sent her both the confession and a deadly powder, hoping that she would use them exactly as she did.

Gryce had said that the paper was the clue to the whole affair, for whoever owned the trimmed sheet was the author of two deaths. He searched Eleanore's writing desk first, to be thorough, and found nothing, but in a drawer of the library table in Mary's own house he discovered a pile of paper whose faint printed lines matched those of the confession precisely. Raymond watched him count the sheets, saw one half-quire that was a sheet short, and felt his heart sink.

Promptly at the appointed hour, Gryce led Raymond past his usual room and up into the garret, where there was nothing but a pine table, two hard chairs and a ring of closed doors with blank round ventilators above them. He begged his companion not to speak, and not to be surprised if he were addressed by some other name, for he was in what he called a facetious mood. The place felt so cold and watchful that Raymond could almost believe that something unearthly was crouching in the air.

Speaking very loudly, as though to a friend called Smith, Gryce declared that he had found the assassin of Mr Leavenworth, and that the culprit was a beautiful and clever woman. After listing every circumstance that pointed toward Eleanore, he swept them all aside and announced that the true criminal was her cousin, the exquisite Mary, and that a report to the police was already being prepared. All the while Raymond felt a strange stir in the air, as if the blank ventilators above the doors were listening.

A door flew open, and Trueman Harwell staggered into the room, begging in a ghastly voice that someone should stop the report and save Mary Leavenworth. At that moment Henry Clavering stepped in through another door, and the secretary, shrieking that he would not hear the stranger call her his wife, flew at his rival's throat. Gryce caught him in a grip that no rheumatism could weaken, and a moment later the man's frame stiffened, as though he saw something dreadful, and he fell to the floor.

In prison, Harwell wrote that he was not a bad man but an intense one, whose passions lay coiled and quiet like serpents that no one suspected. At school and in the store where he worked he had been called dull and mechanical, and from the first evening in the Leavenworth house he had loved Mary with a love that fear and fascination made unbearable. Since she would never stoop to look at him, he wrote, he began to dream of finding some way to become her master.

One day Harwell opened Mr Leavenworth's mail and found a letter signed Henry Ritchie Clavering, hinting that Mary had wronged a man who trusted her. He realised that this letter put Mary's whole future in his hands, but instead of using it at once he gave it to his employer, hoping that the old man's anger would drive her to the edge of ruin. Two days later he dreamed that he stole downstairs with a pistol, and the face of the man in the dream was his own.

On the night of the murder, Harwell heard Mary's dress rustle past his door, and he crept into a closet whose ventilator opened above the library to hear what passed between her and her uncle. He heard Mr Leavenworth, who was in the act of changing his will, answer her plea for forgiveness with the cold words that she had forfeited all his favour. Then he heard her low cry of shame, and he knew in that moment what he meant to do.

When Mary had gone back upstairs, Harwell went calmly down, made a pretext of looking for a lost memorandum book, passed through the passage to the bedroom and brought back the dead man's pistol. He fired at his employer from behind, tore from beneath his hands an unfinished summons to the family lawyer, and thrust it into his pocket with the stained letter from Clavering. For a moment he planned to say that the old man had killed himself, but a glance at the wound told him that no one would believe it.

Needing something to clean the pistol, he picked up a handkerchief from the floor and used it, only afterwards discovering that it belonged to Eleanore, and he thrust it behind a chair cushion. He locked the library door behind him, which was a blunder, and at the top of the stairs he was met by the maid Hannah, who stared at the key in his hand. Taking advantage of her foolish affection for him, he promised to marry her some day, gave her money, and persuaded her to hide with Mrs Belden until the storm should pass.

All night Harwell lay awake with the key and the letters in his hand, and in the morning he hid the key in the gas fixture and made the letter into little lighters in a vase. At the inquest he answered every question as truthfully as he could, but when he saw that suspicion might turn on Mary, he began to lie, and he threw the blame upon Eleanore. The key and the scraps of the letter ended up in Mary's room, and it was there that Eleanore found them and, believing her cousin guilty, took them to protect her.

When Harwell heard Clavering tell Mary that she was his wife, after all he had done to make her free, it was the lightning stroke of his life, and he was almost beside himself with fury. He denounced the newcomer as the murderer in a moment of madness, and when he learned that a servant had seen Clavering enter the house on the night of the crime, he resolved to let the blame fall upon him. One thing stood in his way, and that was Hannah, who alone could tell what she had seen.

Harwell wrote to Hannah in printed capitals, since she could not read handwriting, and played upon her foolish fondness by sending her what he called a charm that would bring beautiful dreams. Inside the envelope he enclosed a powder, which was poison, and a forged confession that threw the blame upon Clavering, and Hannah, trusting him, did exactly as she was told. When the newspaper reported her death, he wrote, he felt no relief at all, and soon afterwards the summons from Gryce arrived.

Raymond hurried to Eleanore and asked her whether she was ready to hear good news, but her burden had lain on her so long that she could not believe that she had nothing to fear. When he told her gently that Trueman Harwell, and not Mary, had caused all the evidence that had troubled her, her first words were a prayer to be taken to the cousin she had wronged. Without waiting to be calm she cried out that she could neither breathe nor think until she had begged for pardon on her knees.

Raymond drove with Eleanore to the house that had seen so much misery, and when she crossed the hall and lifted the curtain, Mary stepped out to meet her. Eleanore fell at her cousin's feet begging pardon, and Mary lifted her with the answer that her own shame was great enough to make her forgive anything. The shadow that had lain for so long between the two women dissolved like a cloud, and the days to come promised confidence and warmth.

A new humility shone in Mary's face as she asked Raymond to help persuade Eleanore to accept the fortune that, by right, should have been hers. Eleanore, firm in her refusal to take property so stained by guilt, would not hear of it, and it was agreed at last that the whole sum should go to a great charity for the unfortunate poor of the city. In this way the fruit of so black a crime was turned, by the generosity of two women, into a lasting good.

Henry Clavering, dignified as ever, drew Raymond aside and apologised for an earlier act that had forced an unwelcome document upon him, an act that he said sprang from mental misery and that he bitterly regretted. Raymond, who had no wish to dwell on bygone miseries, answered that the future promised too richly for them to quarrel over the past, and the two men shook hands in a look of mutual understanding. Mary stood beside her husband, no longer a secret wife, while Eleanore watched with quiet joy.

Mr Veeley deserved to know the truth, for he had grieved like a father over them all, and Mary would gladly have gone to tell him herself, but Eleanore said gently that she had suffered enough. So Raymond and Eleanore left the others in the glow of growing hope and went out together into the night, walking into a dream from which he never woke. Many happy months later, he wrote, the light of her dear eyes was still the guiding star of his life.
